title: Food security remains fragile as fertilizer costs, El Niño risk, and unequal domestic food inflation transmit shocks unevenly across income groups
source_unit: World Bank Food Security Update, latest update June 2026 with data as of 22 June 2026
geography: Global food and nutrition security, domestic food inflation across 169 countries, and income-group and regional exposure

observations.period: First five months of 2026; global fertilizer market

fertilizer_price_change.unit: percent increase in fertilizer prices compared with the first five months of 2025

market_condition.value: fertilizer markets had not fully stabilized by June 2026

lagged_yield_risk.value: reduced applications earlier in the season may become visible later in harvest outcomes

observations.method: The World Bank synthesizes market-monitoring data and food-security analysis, drawing on fertilizer, cereal, food-price, and macro indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Fertilizer prices are not equivalent to farm-gate costs or consumer prices; pass-through depends on crops, subsidies, currency, inventories, and farmer decisions.
observations.subgroup: Fertilizer-importing countries, farmers, food producers, food-importing households, and low-income consumers vulnerable to delayed supply effects.
observations.counterinterpretation: Price pressure can ease before harvest effects appear, and improved efficiency, substitution, stocks, or public support can reduce the impact of expensive inputs.

observations.period: Mid-2026 risk assessment; El Niño probability and cereal exposure

denominator.unit: probability percentage frame for El Niño emergence by mid-2026 and persistence into 2027

el_nino_probability.unit: percent probability of El Niño emerging by mid-2026 and persisting into 2027

rice_output_risk.unit: percent potential decline in rice output in affected regions if the scenario is realized

exposed_regions.value: South Asia, Southern Africa, and parts of East Asia

observations.method: The update combines climate-risk probabilities with agricultural and food-security scenario analysis.
observations.uncertainty: These are conditional risk estimates, not observed output losses; El Niño strength, timing, adaptation, and regional weather determine realized effects.
observations.subgroup: Rice-producing and rice-consuming regions, food-importing governments, smallholder farmers, and already vulnerable households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate signals can also produce favorable conditions in some locations, and reserves, trade, irrigation, crop switching, and safety nets can buffer regional effects.

denominator.unit: countries analyzed in the latest quarterly food-price data

low_income_above_5pct.unit: percent of low-income countries with food inflation above 5%, up from 40.0%

lower_middle_income_above_5pct.unit: percent of lower-middle-income countries with food inflation above 5%, down from 40.8%

upper_middle_income_above_5pct.unit: percent of upper-middle-income countries with food inflation above 5%, down from 34.0%

high_income_above_5pct.unit: percent of high-income countries with food inflation above 5%, down from 6.8%

observations.method: The World Bank compares domestic food inflation across income groups and regions using available country price data.
observations.uncertainty: Country coverage, price baskets, reference periods, exchange rates, and measurement quality vary; country-level inflation does not reveal household diet, income, or coping behavior.
observations.subgroup: Low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income, and high-income country populations, with especially unequal exposure within countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: The decline in higher-income groups and some middle-income groups shows that food-price pressure is not globally uniform and can improve even while low-income-country conditions deteriorate.

observations.period: Latest quarterly data through mid-2026; real food-price pressure

denominator.unit: countries analyzed in the latest quarterly food-price data

real_food_inflation_countries.unit: percent of analyzed countries where real food prices outpaced headline inflation

lower_middle_income_real_food_inflation.unit: lower-middle-income countries recording positive real food inflation

regional_pressure.value: food-inflation pressure increased in Latin America and the Caribbean and South Asia, eased in Europe and Central Asia, and remained uneven across Africa

long_run_price_comparison.value: maize, wheat, and rice prices were 6%, 4%, and 3% above January 2020 levels

observations.method: The update compares food-price inflation with headline inflation to identify real food-price pressure, alongside commodity and regional comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The share of countries is not a share of people or households, and real-price pressure does not identify affordability, nutrition, or food insecurity without income and consumption data.
observations.subgroup: Households with high food-budget shares, lower-middle-income populations, food-importing regions, and countries with limited fiscal space for protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: A country with real food inflation may still protect vulnerable households through transfers, wage growth, local production, or targeted price measures; the aggregate signal identifies exposure, not welfare outcome.

related_sources.claim: Complementary FAO monthly market-price and early-warning evidence.
World Bank agriculture and food-security program context.

boundary: This record adds an income-group and household-risk layer to the food-price route, linking domestic food inflation and real price pressure to fertilizer costs, El Niño scenarios, cereal production, and regional inequality. It uses country-level aggregate and conditional scenario evidence, not household purchase histories, diet records, individual food-security transitions, causal welfare estimates, or proof that food insecurity changed for every group.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: World Bank Food Security Update page and linked June 2026 brief were reviewed for fertilizer prices, El Niño probabilities, rice-output scenarios, income-group food inflation, real food prices, commodity comparisons, and data boundaries.
